week.t: NHC: no tropical cyclones in the Atlantic and none expected for 7 days; one hurricane all season
NASA asks industry about a commercial mission to service Hubble before it re-enters around 2033–2034
Menon and Kutryk install the seventh roll-out solar array in a 7 h 11 min spacewalk
Science News: Malagasy flying foxes have skulls 6 percent smaller than before the 1980s
Earth Observatory: Landsat 9’s view of Chiricahua, redesignated a national park in October
NTU and VFT launch a S$15 million joint lab for flow batteries

tiles.cap: Two astronauts spent 7 h 11 min outside the ISS fitting a solar array. Next one: Thursday
tiles.nums: the station’s power once all eight roll-out arrays are in, up from 160 kW: an increase of up to 30%
tiles.p1: NASA astronaut Anil Menon and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk concluded their spacewalk outside the International Space Station at 3:08 p.m. EDT on 29 October, which is 3:08 on Friday morning in Singapore. During the 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk they installed and deployed an International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (IROSA) on the station’s 2A electrical power channel, the seventh IROSA installed on the station. It was U.S. spacewalk 100, Menon’s fourth and Kutryk’s first, and the 285th spacewalk in support of station assembly, maintenance and upgrades.
tiles.p2: Why it matters to you: the eighth and final IROSA goes on the 3B power channel in a spacewalk planned for Thursday 5 November, with NASA’s live coverage beginning at 6:45 a.m. (US Eastern time, which by then has gone back to standard time: 7:45 pm in Singapore).
deep: Riding the arm

The photo on this tile is NASA’s: Menon rides the Canadarm2 robotic arm to begin the installation of the roll-out solar array on the station’s port-side truss structure, while orbiting 260 miles above Earth.
How the array got there
The final pair of roll-out arrays flew up in the SpaceX Dragon cargo ship that launched on NASA’s 35th commercial resupply mission at 6:33 a.m. EDT on 13 October.
The power arithmetic

NASA: together, the eight arrays will increase available power by up to 30%, boosting the station’s power generation capacity from 160 kilowatts to approximately 215 kilowatts. Check it yourself: 215 divided by 160 comes to a little more than 1.3, so NASA’s “up to 30%” is a rounded figure.
Get-ahead work
Menon and Kutryk also completed several get-ahead tasks to prepare for the 5 November spacewalk. Watching the second one live is a Thursday-evening plan.
tiles.src: NASA Space Station blog, 29 Oct 2026 (Mark A. Garcia) · NASA release, 13 Oct 2026

tiles.cap: NASA asks companies: can you fly up and save Hubble before it falls to Earth, around 2033?
tiles.nums: the year by which NASA anticipates a servicing mission would need to take place
tiles.p1: On Friday 30 October NASA said it had issued a Request for Information on 29 October, asking industry about potential commercial servicing of the Hubble Space Telescope. NASA’s analysis predicts Hubble is likely to re-enter the atmosphere in the 2033 to 2034 timeframe, so a mission would need to take place by 2032. Responses are open until 3 p.m. EST on Monday 30 November.
tiles.p2: Why now: in Nicky Fox’s words, Hubble has fundamentally changed how humanity views our universe for more than 35 years; it has been operating for more than three decades; NASA’s own prediction gives it well under a decade before re-entry.
deep: What a Request for Information is
It is not a contract. NASA describes what it needs, companies describe what they could do and roughly what it would take, and NASA uses the answers to decide whether and how to buy a mission.
The photo
NASA’s caption: the Hubble Space Telescope returns to orbit as an improved telescope after its second servicing mission in February 1997.
Who is involved

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and Nicky Fox, associate administrator of the Science Mission Directorate, are quoted in the announcement. Hubble is a project of international cooperation between NASA and ESA.

tiles.cap: Arizona’s new national park: rock pillars from an eruption 1,000 times Mount St. Helens
tiles.nums: years ago, the eruptions in what is now southeastern Arizona that laid down the rock
tiles.p1: Some 27 million years ago, a volcano in what is now southeastern Arizona unleashed a series of eruptions, strewing more than 1,000 times as much volcanic material across the landscape as Mount St. Helens did in 1980. In some areas the deposits were nearly 1,600 feet (500 meters) thick. Erosion since then has carved them into a maze of pinnacles and balanced rocks. The area was designated a national monument in 1924 and in October 2026 it was redesignated as Chiricahua National Park.
tiles.p2: Why this picture: the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured a cloud-free image of the new national park on 2 July 2026; NASA’s Earth Observatory published it on Wednesday 28 October.
deep: The hole it left
The eruptions left the Turkey Creek caldera, roughly 12 miles (19 kilometers) wide and 4,900 feet (1,500 meters) deep.
Four worlds meet

Four biogeographic regions converge in the park: the Sonoran Desert, the Chihuahuan Desert, the Rocky Mountains and the Sierra Madre. The range’s highest point, just outside the park, rises 2,986 meters (9,795 feet) above sea level, more than 1,800 meters above the surrounding valley.
Standing-up rocks

The park lies on the traditional lands of the Chiricahua Apache, and the Earth Observatory’s title calls it the land of the standing-up rocks. Big Balanced Rock has a surprisingly large boulder precariously perched on top; hiking through Rhyolite Canyon or driving through Bonita Canyon means a dizzying maze of pinnacles.
Reading the image

In the satellite view the park boundary is outlined; grey ridges are cut by green, vegetated canyons, and to the west the land is flatter, redder and less vegetated. Credit: NASA Earth Observatory image by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey.
tiles.credit: Photo: NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey

tiles.cap: The Atlantic has produced one hurricane all year. The Pacific had an 892-millibar monster
tiles.nums: hurricane in the Atlantic in 2026 so far: Isaias, 6–10 October, 105 knots, 959 mb
tiles.p1: The US National Hurricane Center’s season table (as of 21 UTC on 31 October) lists ten named Atlantic systems in 2026: nine tropical or subtropical storms and a single hurricane, Isaias, a major hurricane that peaked at 105 knots (about 195 km/h) with a central pressure of 959 millibars. The latest, Subtropical Storm Josephine, lasted from 21 to 22 October. The eastern Pacific table runs to 22 systems, including Polo (20–29 September), which peaked at 155 knots (about 287 km/h) and 892 millibars.
tiles.p2: Why now: NHC’s Saturday 31 October outlook says tropical cyclone formation is not expected in the Atlantic during the next 7 days; the eastern Pacific gives a 40 percent chance of a system forming well southeast of Hawaii within 7 days.
deep: Knots and millibars
Forecasters give wind in knots (nautical miles per hour; 1 knot is 1.852 km/h) and pressure in millibars. Polo’s 892 mb is the lowest pressure in either table.
What “major” means
NHC’s table defines a major hurricane as one with winds of 96 knots or higher. Isaias at 105 knots qualifies; none of the other nine Atlantic systems reached hurricane strength at all.
The season’s calendar

The Atlantic list began with Tropical Storm Arthur on 17–18 June and includes Bertha, Cristobal, Dolly, Edouard, Fay, Gonzalo, Hanna, Isaias and Josephine. Fay lasted longest, 19 to 29 September, peaking at 60 knots.
Meanwhile, nearer home

Cyclone Arnab, the first named storm of the 2026 North Indian Ocean cyclone season, emerged in the Bay of Bengal on 25 October and made landfall on the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coast early on 28 October with sustained winds of 130 kilometres per hour, similar to a Category 1 storm on the Saffir-Simpson scale, per NASA’s Earth Observatory.
tiles.src: NOAA National Hurricane Center: 2026 season tables and Tropical Weather Outlooks, 30–31 Oct 2026 · NASA Earth Observatory, 29 Oct 2026

tiles.cap: A battery that lives in tanks of non-flammable liquid, not a sealed cell: NTU’s S$15m lab
tiles.nums: the four-year NTU-VFT joint lab for vanadium redox flow batteries, announced 27 October
tiles.p1: Nanyang Technological University, through its Energy Research Institute @ NTU (ERI@N), and the company VFT have launched a S$15 million joint research laboratory to develop safer, more durable and cost-effective batteries for the power grid. The lab works on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs), which use non-flammable, aqueous-based liquids to store energy, significantly reducing the risk of battery fires compared with conventional lithium-ion batteries. VRFBs store energy in liquid electrolytes held in external tanks, and their storage capacity can be increased by using larger tanks.
tiles.p2: Why here: VFT’s CEO, Dr Vidal Bharath, puts it this way: “The challenge is no longer simply generating more renewable energy.” Power systems also need safe ways to store it. The lab was launched at the Asia Clean Energy Summit, held as part of Singapore International Energy Week 2026.
deep: Why tanks
Because the energy is in the liquid, not in the cell, a bigger tank means more hours of storage. That is the opposite of a phone battery, where everything is sealed in one package.
The spin-off
Founded in 2018, VFT is an NTU spin-off based on technology developed at ERI@N. The company raised US$20.5 million in 2025 to expand manufacturing and deployment of its flow-battery systems.
What the lab will do

Researchers will develop more powerful and efficient flow batteries and use artificial intelligence to monitor battery performance, detect faults and predict maintenance needs. The collaboration is supported under Singapore’s Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2025 plans.
In their words

Professor Madhavi Srinivasan, Executive Director of ERI@N: “we aim to develop safer, longer-lasting and sustainable batteries to power our future energy grid.” The four-year collaboration runs through ERI@N.

tiles.cap: An IIT Bombay rig pulls up to 3 tonnes of CO₂ a day from factory emissions and the air
tiles.nums: of carbon dioxide per day that India’s first integrated CCUS field laboratory at IIT Bombay can capture
tiles.p1: CCUS stands for carbon capture, utilisation and storage. Capture systems separate carbon dioxide from gases released during fuel combustion or industrial processes; the captured gas is then either put to productive use or stored permanently underground, injected deep into suitable geological formations. India’s first integrated CCUS field laboratory at IIT Bombay, inaugurated in May 2026, is an indigenous facility that can capture up to 3 tonnes of carbon dioxide per day from industrial emissions and ambient air, and converts it into carbonate and bicarbonate products.
tiles.p2: Why now: a PIB backgrounder on 27 October 2026, drawing on Department of Science and Technology programmes, sets out the plan: a national CCUS roadmap launched in December 2025, and ₹20,000 crore allocated over five years in the Union Budget 2026–27.
deep: Where the CO₂ comes from

As of August 2026, fossil-fuel sources accounted for 45.12% of India’s total installed power capacity. Industry is the other big source, which is why the first cluster of five carbon capture and utilisation testbeds is for the cement industry.
The centres

Two national CCUS centres were established in 2022, at IIT Bombay and at JNCASR in Bengaluru. As of April 2026 the backgrounder counts three projects operational, six under construction and sixteen at the proposed stage. Scientific drilling in Deccan Traps basalt formations will further assess India’s potential for safe and permanent carbon dioxide storage.
The target
India’s journey towards Net Zero by 2070 requires reducing emissions across its energy and industrial sectors; capture is meant for the emissions that are hardest to design away.
Think it through
Three tonnes a day is a test size, not a power-station size. A field laboratory’s job is to prove the chemistry and the costs at a scale that can be copied, which is what the cement testbeds are for.
tiles.src: PIB backgrounder, 27 Oct 2026, drawing on Department of Science and Technology programmes

tiles.cap: Swing a bottle of water on a string. Pour out half the water: the timing does not change
tiles.nums: swings in 30 seconds for a 38.7 cm pendulum, the longest in the Exploratorium’s Pendulum Snake
tiles.p1: The time a pendulum takes for one swing depends on its length and on gravity, and on nothing else: T = 2π√(L/g), where T is the period in seconds per swing, L is the length in metres and g is the acceleration due to gravity, 9.8 m/s². The mass cancels out of the equation, so pendulums of different masses but the same length behave identically, and for small swings the size of the swing does not matter either. Galileo was the first to record that the period of a swinging lamp high in a cathedral was independent of the amplitude of the oscillations, at least for the small amplitudes he could observe.
tiles.p2: Test it, as the Exploratorium suggests: swing a bottle of water on a string, first full, then with half the water dumped out; then try little swings and big, wide swings. Does the period change? Counting swings in 30 seconds each time will tell you.
deep: The number on this tile

The Exploratorium’s longest pendulum swings back and forth 24 times in 30 seconds, which is 0.8 swings per second. Put 9.8 m/s² and 0.8 swings per second into the formula and you get a length of 0.387 metres, or 38.7 centimetres. Its shortest, 20.5 cm, makes 33 swings in the same 30 seconds.
Galileo’s pulse

Feynman tells it in Chapter 5 of his Lectures: Galileo’s first experiments on motion were done by using his pulse to count off equal intervals of time. He decided that a given pendulum always swings back and forth in equal intervals of time so long as the size of the swing is kept small; count 3600 swings in an hour and each period is one second.
The first real clock

In 1657 Huygens constructed the first pendulum clock, a vast improvement in timekeeping over all previous techniques, so the pendulum was the first oscillator of real technological importance. Today’s version is electrical: Feynman calls oscillators “electrical pendulums”, a current swinging to and fro.
Where the rule bends

Michael Fowler of the University of Virginia: the pendulum is not quite a simple harmonic oscillator; the period does depend on the amplitude, but provided the angular amplitude is kept small this is a small effect. Your wide swings should run very slightly slower.
tiles.src: Exploratorium Science Snacks: Pendulum Snake · The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I, Ch. 5 · Michael Fowler, University of Virginia, Physics 152: The Pendulum

tiles.cap: One muon crosses your hand about every second. On paper, almost none should reach you
tiles.nums: a muon’s mean lifetime at rest: at nearly the speed of light, that is only about 660 metres of travel
tiles.p1: Cosmic rays from space collide with atoms 15 to 20 kilometres up in the atmosphere. The collisions create pions, which decay into muons. A muon has a measured mean lifetime of about 2.2 microseconds; even at the speed of light it would travel on average only about 660 metres before decaying. From 15 km up, the trip takes 50 microseconds, more than twenty lifetimes, so almost no muons should reach the ground. Yet they arrive at ground level at about one per square centimetre per minute.
tiles.p2: The explanation is Einstein’s: time ticks slowly for particles moving at speeds close to that of light. In MIT’s version of the sum, a muon at 0.998 times the speed of light has a time-stretch factor of 15, and about one muon travels through your hand every second.
deep: The factor

The stretch is the Lorentz factor, 1/√(1 − v²/c²). For a 20 GeV muon, the CERN page gets it from E = mc²: the muon’s rest mass is 106 MeV, so the factor is 20 GeV divided by 106 MeV, which is 189. Its lifetime, as we see it, becomes 189 × 2.2 microseconds, and a significant fraction of the muons made in the upper atmosphere reach the ground.
MIT’s version

Prof. Markus Klute’s MIT lecture on muons: the lifetime is about 2.2 microseconds, the muons are produced at close to the speed of light, 0.998 times it, the classical distance works out to about 660 metres, and the gamma factor is 15; the clock in the muon, as observed by us, ticks much, much slower than for a muon at rest.
Muons as X-rays

Physics World: as many as 10,000 muons rain down on each square metre every minute, and muons at shallow angles can travel as far as 300 km before hitting the ground. Because they pass through rock, detectors placed beside volcanoes such as Sakurajima in Japan image the magma conduits inside, a technique called muography.
Discovery

Victor Hess found cosmic rays on a balloon flight in 1912, measuring the rate of ionisation as he ascended to 5300 metres. The muon itself was identified in 1937. At rest, CERN notes, it decays after only 2.2 microseconds into an electron and two kinds of neutrinos.
tiles.src: CERN High School Teachers programme: cosmic ray muons and relativistic time dilation · MIT OpenCourseWare 8.20, Prof. Markus Klute · Physics World, 25 Jul 2023 (Michael Allen) · home.cern

tiles.cap: A camera with a printer inside: 16 seconds a print, 15-second films, a dial of ten decades
tiles.nums: the print head’s resolution: 1600 × 600 dots exposed onto instax mini film in about 16 seconds
tiles.p1: Fujifilm’s Instax Mini Evo Cinema, in TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026, is two machines in one 270 g body styled like a Super 8 film camera. The camera half is a 1/5-inch CMOS sensor of approximately 5 million pixels behind an f/2.0 lens equivalent to 28 mm, recording 1920 × 2560 stills and 15-second video clips at 24 frames per second (600 × 800 in standard mode; 1080 × 1440 in a high-quality mode that works only with the 2020 setting and records to microSD) to internal memory or a microSD card up to 256 GB. The printer half exposes the digital image onto chemical instax mini film at 1600 × 600 dots, 40 × 80 µm per dot, in about 16 seconds; a full charge is good for approximately 100 prints.
tiles.p2: What reviewers found wrong: TechRadar’s Timothy Coleman, after two weeks, called operation “pretty sluggish”, saw a loading wheel almost every time he recorded a video or switched eras, had the camera freeze once until the battery drained, and judged the video “lo-fi at just HD 720p”; his cons list reads sluggish operation, poor image quality, video clip length limitations, pricey. Tom’s Guide’s Nikita Achanta found the print lever finicky and the camera expensive: US$409 at Tom’s Guide, US$419 at TechRadar.
deep: Why the print looks like film

The print is a real photochemical picture: instead of light from a lens, the print head exposes the instax film from the digital file, at 1600 × 600 dots. The print is only 1600 × 600 dots, far fewer than the sensor’s 1920 × 2560.
The Gen Dial

Twist it before shooting to apply one of ten effects named for the decades 1930 to 2020, inspired by a century of film formats, each with a degree control. The 1.54-inch LCD has approximately 170,000 dots and is not touch-sensitive.
The numbers that limit it

Shutter 1/4 to 1/8000 second and ISO 100 to 1600, both automatic. Video bitrate is 2.5 Mbps in standard mode and 9.0 Mbps in high quality, and each clip stops at about 15 seconds; internal memory holds approximately 50 shots and 10 clips. Charging takes 2 to 3 hours over USB-C, which is for charging only.
The verdict split

Coleman: “Technically speaking, this is a poor camera”, yet it still won his heart. Achanta: “one of the best instant cameras you can buy right now, period.” Both call it expensive; Achanta still lists its image and print quality as a plus.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Kevin Cortez) · Fujifilm specifications page · TechRadar (Timothy Coleman, updated 17 Feb 2026) · Tom’s Guide (Nikita Achanta, 4 Feb 2026)

tiles.cap: Eyes closed, hands up: touch your nose, then each fingertip of the other hand. Then wiggle
tiles.p1: Close your eyes and raise both hands above your head. Keep the fingers of your left hand totally still. With your right hand, quickly touch your index fingertip to your nose, then quickly touch the tip of your left thumb with the tip of your right index finger. Repeat, returning to your nose in between, trying to land on each fingertip in turn. Switch hands and try again. How many did you hit? Now try once more while wiggling the fingers of the raised hand.
tiles.p2: What is going on: even with your eyes closed you have a sense of body position. Muscles, tendons, joints and the inner ear contain proprioceptors, also known as stretch receptors, which relay positional information to your brain. Wiggling the fingers sends extra information, which is why the second round usually goes better.
deep: Why you miss

Most of us are highly dependent on visual cues for judging distance and position, so proprioception alone is not enough to give the fine detail these tasks need. With repeated tries you can learn to do them better.
X marks the spot

Hold a sheet of paper on the table, mark an X, raise the pencil hand above your head, close your eyes and try to put a dot on the X. Open your eyes, check, and try again several times, then repeat with your eyes open; looking at the position of the X between tries helps you adjust.
Handwriting with eyes shut

Write the word proprioception on a lined sheet, then write it again next to it with your eyes closed. Most people find vision is not an important cue for writing, because the feel of writing comes from proprioceptors in the hands and fingers.
Where it goes

The Exploratorium links this to Dr. Patricia Cowings, a psychophysiologist who trained as an astronaut at NASA and was an alternate to go into space in 1979; she developed individually tailored protocols to prevent motion sickness in astronauts, and her Autogenic Feedback Training, known by the initials AFTE, has been used widely.

tiles.cap: Bats with 1.5 m wingspans are shrinking: skulls 6 percent smaller than before the 1980s
tiles.nums: museum specimens of the Malagasy flying fox, stored in nine museums, measured for the paper
tiles.p1: Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus), fruit bats of Madagascar with a leathery wingspan of up to a metre and a half, have skulls that are 6 percent smaller than they were prior to the 1980s. The first hints came from scientific collections at the Field Museum in Chicago, where flying vertebrate ecologist Emily Cornelius Ruhs and conservation biologist Steven Goodman noticed something strange. They recorded 12 skull and tooth features on 121 specimens stored in nine museums, collected over more than 150 years; skulls from before the 1980s averaged 3.6 millimetres longer, about 6 percent, than those collected after.
tiles.p2: Why: possible causes included climate change or habitat loss, but the timing lines up with the commercialisation of flying fox hunting. Until the 1980s the animals were mostly hunted on a very small scale to feed a family or small community; as hunting pressure increased, the biggest bats may have been selectively targeted.
deep: The drawer evidence
Two Field Museum specimens tell it side by side: a bat collected in 1948 next to a visibly smaller one collected in 1995. Museum drawers are time machines for exactly this kind of question.
How many are left

There were an estimated 300,000 Malagasy flying foxes in Madagascar in the early 2000s; researchers estimate the number has dropped by two-thirds since then. “Bats are eaten in Madagascar in certain villages and cultures,” Ruhs says.
Why size matters
Emma Stone, a conservation biologist at the University of Bath: “Species are specifically adapted to their environments and adaptation takes place over thousands of years.”
Next
Future work on the bats’ genetics could tell researchers how modern populations are faring, Ruhs says. The paper, “Shrinking giants”, was published in the Journal of Mammalogy on 29 October 2026.
tiles.src: Science News, 29 Oct 2026 (Jake Buehler) · Ruhs & Goodman, Journal of Mammalogy, 2026

tiles.cap: From 18 November, a radio message to Voyager 1 will take a full day to arrive
tiles.nums: Voyager 1’s speed (61,155 km/h); it is 16 billion miles (24 billion km) from Earth
tiles.p1: NASA said on Thursday 29 October that engineers had turned off three devices on Voyager 1 and substituted three lower-power alternatives, a swap the team nicknamed the “Big Bang”, done in early September about six weeks after a similar swap on Voyager 2. With their plutonium supply continually depleting, both probes lose about 4 watts of power each year. The mission launched in 1977 with 10 dedicated science instruments; the team had already been forced to turn off two, and without the swap another would have followed as early as summer 2027.
tiles.p2: Also in the report: contact with Voyager 1 was lost on 18 and 19 October during two scheduled contact attempts 24 hours apart, and the signal returned on 20 October. One group of thrusters had gone offline and backups activated automatically, a response known as fault protection. The root cause is still being investigated. Kareem Badaruddin, the Voyager mission manager at JPL, on the signal loss: “We’re relieved to be back in contact with Voyager 1 and are eager to understand what happened.”
deep: One light-day

On 18 November Voyager 1 will be one light-day away: 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion km). NASA: “That means that the radio waves used to communicate with the probe take 24 hours to reach it.” Suzanne Dodd, the Voyager project manager at JPL: “If you want to say ‘hello’ to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response.”
Why swap rather than switch off

The Big Bang was unique because the three swaps had to happen simultaneously: only by swapping all three could the team both cut the power Voyager 1 uses and make sure heat is properly distributed on the spacecraft.
The farthest thing we have made

NASA calls Voyager 1 the spacecraft that has travelled farther than any other human-made object. The photo on this tile was taken on 27 April 1977 and shows one of the Voyagers in the 25-Foot Space Simulator at JPL, before launch.
Check the arithmetic
Light covers about 300,000 km every second. Multiply by the 86,400 seconds in a day and compare your answer with 25.89 billion km.

tiles.cap: Curiosity is firing 150 laser shots into one spot, next to the rock it plans to drill
tiles.nums: Martian days (sols) into Curiosity’s mission when it took this close-up, on 18 October 2026
tiles.p1: NASA’s Curiosity blog for sols 5043 to 5049, posted on Wednesday 28 October by planetary scientist Lucy Lim of NASA Goddard, says that after the Basque Lakes drill campaign the rover has returned to a spot just a few metres from the Chiu Chiu block. A block called Chiu Chiu was not a good drill candidate, but the block just beyond it was much more promising; it is now named Nazca, and it is “jam-packed” with disc- and needle-shaped lumps; one leading idea is that the shapes were created as crystals grew. ChemCam is concentrating all 150 of its laser shots on the same spot of a nearby crystal-form-rich target called Toucan.
tiles.p2: Why 150 shots in one place: a normal ChemCam observation is a five-point raster with 30 shots per point. The 150-shot profile should penetrate approximately five times deeper into the rock.
deep: Pictures first

MAHLI, the camera on the arm, takes five overlapping images at slightly different geometries for a Quantitative Relief Model of the surface, and doubles its focus steps for its highest-resolution imaging. The photo on this tile is MAHLI’s close-up of the disc-shaped lumps on Nazca, with scratches from the Dust Removal Tool.
Before the drill

LIBS, the Dust Removal Tool and the APXS spectrometer will all be applied to the Nazca spot before the preload test. The third laser target in the plan, Condor, is a nearby block with a finely layered texture exposed.
Clouds over Mars
Twilight cloud season is beginning, and Curiosity is imaging Phobos, the larger and brighter of Mars’ two moons, at night to estimate the sizes of particles in high-altitude carbon dioxide clouds.
tiles.src: NASA Curiosity mission blog, 28 Oct 2026 (Lucy Lim)

tiles.cap: A gaming PC in a 6-inch cube. One big slow fan keeps it quiet; 4K is where it struggles
tiles.nums: the fan Valve built the Steam Machine around: a cube just large enough to hold it, cooling an AMD CPU and GPU
tiles.p1: Valve’s Steam Machine, in TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026, is a six-inch cube. Valve hardware engineer Yazan Aldehayyat says the team wanted a computer powerful enough to run complex game engines and vivid open worlds but compact enough for a desk or TV stand; making it a six-inch cube just large enough to host a 120 mm fan solved both. That fan cools the AMD CPU and GPU at much lower speeds than a laptop’s, so the Machine is quiet enough for a living room. Inside, per Valve’s store page: a semi-custom AMD Zen 4 processor with 6 cores and 12 threads, a semi-custom RDNA3 graphics chip with 28 compute units, 16 GB of DDR5 memory plus 8 GB of GDDR6 video memory, a 512 GB or 2 TB NVMe SSD, Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3, running SteamOS 3. Price and date were announced on 22 June 2026; it went on sale at the end of June 2026 from US$1,049.
tiles.p2: What reviewers found wrong: TechRadar’s Christian Guyton (25 July 2026, 3.33 out of 5) called it “seriously expensive even when compared to full-fat desktop PCs”, found performance “great at 1080p, decent at 1440p, and decidedly mixed at 4K” (Cyberpunk 2077: 71 fps at 1080p Ultra, 17 fps at 4K Ultra), and his cons included the Steam Controller sold separately and games locked to Steam by default; he also noted a single USB-C port at the rear, no Wi-Fi 7 and a small number of crashes.
deep: Why one big fan is quiet

TIME’s explanation: the 120 mm fan cools the CPU and GPU at much lower speeds than those you would typically find in a laptop, which keeps the Machine quiet enough to actually use in a living room. Guyton agreed, calling the fan whisper-quiet.
Two kinds of memory

The 16 GB of DDR5 is the system memory the processor works in; the 8 GB of GDDR6 is video memory for the graphics chip. Guyton wrote that “the ongoing RAM crisis has taken a toll on the Steam Machine’s value proposition”.
Why 4K hurts

A 4K frame has four times the pixels of a 1080p frame, so the same chip has four times as much to draw. Guyton’s table shows it: Shadow of the Tomb Raider 131 fps at 1080p Highest, 47 fps at 4K Highest; Total War: Warhammer III 58 fps at 1080p Ultra, 24 fps at 4K Ultra.
Size and price

15.2 × 16.2 × 15.6 cm and 2.60 kg, with a 17-LED light bar, HDMI 2.0 and one DisplayPort 1.4. You can swap the SSD and the RAM, but that is it. The 2 TB model is US$1,349, and the controller adds US$79 in a bundle (US$99 on its own).
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Kevin Cortez) · Steam store page · TechRadar, 25 Jul 2026 (Christian Guyton)

tiles.cap: MIT’s phrase for what a chatbot answer gives you: “the illusion of learning”
tiles.nums: principles in MIT’s 2026 report on AI in education
tiles.p1: MIT’s report does not ban AI. One of its eight principles is augmentation, not automation: AI should be used to “augment and enhance curiosity, creativity, and learning, not automate them.” Its named risks are the ones you would expect, weaker memory and confidence, falling back on AI at the first hint of struggle, and one you might not: fewer people. MIT saw fewer students at office hours and, anecdotally, fewer in-person groups in dorms and libraries, turning to AI instead of to classmates, TAs or professors.
tiles.p2: The point: the product of school is you, not the mark.
deep: What MIT asks of its own students
Learn to write good prompts, check every output, recognise when it has made something up, and know when not to use it at all.
Why checking matters
The report warns that models hallucinate, so students need to learn when an output is likely to be made up. MIT’s rule for research: a human verifies, and AI is never listed as a co-author.
Keep it human

The report says every subject should include a regular in-person social component, calls for more project-based work, and asks for deliberately AI-free experiences and AI-free spaces for interaction and assessment.
